title: Blood and water (John 19:31–37)
hookLine: a soldier pierces his side; the Fathers saw baptism and the Eucharist flow out
last: HE TOOK HER TO HIS OWN.

cards: There's a detail on many crucifixes that's easy to walk past: a wound in the right side, under the ribs. Sometimes it's just a red line. Some old paintings show a thin stream running from it, caught in a cup by an angel.
In the Divine Mercy image, two rays, one pale and one red, pour out from that same place. All of it comes from a single moment, after Jesus has already died, that John says an eyewitness swore to.

teach.b: It's Friday, the day of preparation, and the sabbath about to begin is, John says, a great sabbath day.
The authorities don't want bodies on crosses over the holy day, so they ask Pilate to have the legs broken to hasten death. The soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus.
When they come to him, he's already dead.
Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water."
John stops the story to swear to it: the one who saw it has given testimony, and his testimony is true, so that you also may believe. Why does it matter so much?
Partly, it shows he was truly dead, against anyone who'd say otherwise.
Partly, John sees scripture fulfilled: not a bone of him shall be broken, as with the Passover lamb, and from Zechariah, "They shall look on him whom they pierced." But the early Church saw more.
Notice the Douay's word, opened, which follows the Latin. Saint Augustine noticed it too.
He wrote that the evangelist chose the word opened because there the door of life was opened, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed out: water for baptism, blood for the Eucharist.
Some of the Fathers added a picture from Genesis: as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, the Church was born from the side of Christ asleep on the cross.
The Catechism repeats that image. That's why Catholics look so carefully at that wound.

how: Catholics honor the pierced heart of Jesus on the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart, and some pray before the Divine Mercy image, whose two rays stand for the blood and water.

o: the spear's work, a door of life for Augustine
torn by nails as he hung on the cross
the tomb's stone rolled back on Easter

s: the soldier pierced Jesus's side before he died

games.q: you're a Roman soldier. the other two men are still alive and you've broken their legs. the man in the middle seems already dead. what do you do?
o: open his side with a spear.
leave him and report to Pilate.
games.why: they don't break his legs. a soldier opens his side with a spear, and immediately there came out blood and water.

practice: If there's a crucifix near you, look at it; if not, find an image or simply picture one, and let your eyes go to the side, the wound under the ribs, traditionally on the right.

Stay there without analyzing, just looking, the way John says the world will look on him. If you pray, let Zechariah's line be the whole prayer, they shall look on him whom they pierced; if you don't, simply look, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Opened. The Douay's word for the spear in Jesus's side, which Augustine called the door of life, from which flowed the water and blood of the sacraments. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: they shall look on him. Water and blood, from one opened side. That's day five hundred thirty.
